correct_answer: By the time the bus pulled into the parking lot, the first bell had already sounded, so Marco hurried to class.
error_sites: past perfect 'had already sounded' for the action finished before the bus arrived
past tense 'hurried' to match the rest of the past-tense sentence

student_error.By the time the bus pulled into the park: uses simple past for the earlier action, not seeing that 'By the time ... pulled in' calls for 'had sounded'
slips into the present ('hurries') in the last clause, far from the past-tense verbs at the start, as in telling a story aloud
tells the events in the order they happened without marking time: simple past for the earlier action, then a slip into the present at the end

correct_answer: By the time the parents arrive at three o'clock tomorrow, the team will have finished cleaning up the soccer field.
error_sites: present tense 'arrive' in a 'by the time' clause about the future
future perfect 'will have finished' in the main clause

student_error.By the time the parents will arrive at t: puts 'will' in the time clause because the arrival is in the future
student_error.By the time the parents arrive at three: uses the present perfect 'has finished' for a completed action, missing that the finishing point is tomorrow
student_error.By the time the parents will arrive at t: uses 'will' where the future seems to belong and the present perfect for 'finished', without matching either verb to 'by the time ... tomorrow'

explanation: A clause beginning 'By the time' that refers to the future uses the present tense ('arrive'), and an action that will be complete before then takes the future perfect ('will have finished'). 'will arrive' is wrong in the time clause, and 'has finished' cannot describe something completed by a time that is still tomorrow.
varied_dimension: present tense in a 'by the time' clause about the future; future perfect (not present perfect) in the main clause

correct_answer: Coach Ruiz not only reminded us to stretch but also warned that neither the gym nor the pool would open Monday.
error_sites: 'not only' placed before the verb 'reminded' to match 'but also warned'
'nor' as the partner of 'neither'

student_error.Coach Ruiz reminded us not only to stret: puts 'not only' after 'reminded us', so it is followed by 'to stretch' while 'but also' is followed by the verb 'warned'
student_error.Coach Ruiz not only reminded us to stret: pairs 'neither' with 'or', the way 'either ... or' works
student_error.Coach Ruiz reminded us not only to stret: does not know that correlative pairs must match: misplaces 'not only' and pairs 'neither' with 'or'

explanation: 'Not only' and 'but also' must sit before the same kind of word: 'not only reminded ... but also warned' (two verbs). 'Neither' always pairs with 'nor'. The other options either set 'not only to stretch' against 'but also warned' or use 'neither ... or'.
varied_dimension: placement of 'not only' so both halves match; 'nor' as the partner of 'neither'

student_error.Last summer my cousins stayed with us, a: writes 'wakes up' because the 'before' clause sounds like a daily routine, shifting out of the past

choices: Despite the field was still muddy, the game went on because of the referee's decision that the grass was safe enough.
Although the field was still muddy, the game went on because the referee's decision that the grass was safe enough.
Despite the field was still muddy, the game went on because the referee's decision that the grass was safe enough.
Although the field was still muddy, the game went on because of the referee's decision that the grass was safe enough.
correct_answer: Although the field was still muddy, the game went on because of the referee's decision that the grass was safe enough.
error_sites: the conjunction 'Although' before a full clause
the preposition 'because of' (not the conjunction 'because') before a noun phrase

student_error.Despite the field was still muddy, the g: uses the preposition 'Despite' as if it were a conjunction, because it means about the same as 'Although'
student_error.Although the field was still muddy, the: uses the conjunction 'because' before a noun phrase ('the referee's decision'), as if a clause followed
student_error.Despite the field was still muddy, the g: does not tell conjunctions from prepositions, so uses each where the other belongs: 'Despite' before a clause and 'because' before a noun phrase

explanation: A full clause with its own subject and verb ('the field was still muddy') must follow a conjunction such as 'Although'; 'Despite' is a preposition and needs a noun ('Despite the mud'). A noun phrase ('the referee's decision') must follow a preposition such as 'because of'; the conjunction 'because' needs a full clause.
varied_dimension: conjunction vs preposition before a clause ('Although' vs 'Despite'); preposition vs conjunction before a noun phrase ('because of' vs 'because')

student_error.Since joining the chess club in Septembe: uses simple past with 'Since ... September', which describes time up to now

varied_dimension: present perfect with 'since'; simple past (not past perfect) with a finished time ('last week')
